screens.title: Unit Testing with unittest
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you'll build fluency with Python's built-in unittest framework and learn why xUnit-style tests matter for robust, maintainable code. We will explore the TestCase pattern, the convention of test_ methods used by discovery, and a broad set of assertion helpers that let you express expectations clearly. You'll also learn how to manage test fixtures with setUp and tearDown so each test runs in isolation, and when to use class-level setup for expensive shared resources. Along the way we practice with concrete examples: a BankAccount class for numeric operations and a StringUtilities palindrome checker for string edge cases. By mastering unittest you gain a standard-library skill that helps debug regressions, document intended behaviour, and support continuous integration. This lesson prepares you to write focused tests, avoid common mistakes like forgetting to inherit from TestCase, and organize tests so they run smoothly from the command line. As you move forward, ask yourself: does each test verify one behavior and clean up after itself?

Module 10 › Chapter 10.2 › Unit Testing with unittest
Unit Testing with unittest

Master TestCase classes, fixtures, assertions, discovery, and practical test organization using only the standard library.

In this lesson

Learn TestCase basics, fixtures with setUp/tearDown, assertions, test discovery, and common mistakes using concrete examples.

Coming up

Code walkthroughs for BankAccount and StringUtilities, and how to run tests from the CLI.

Explore Key Topics
TestCase Pattern
Inherit unittest.TestCase, name methods test_*, use assertion helpers to express expectations.
Fixtures
setUp and tearDown run before and after each test; class-level methods run once per class.
Running Tests
Use python -m unittest with discover-friendly filenames like test_*.py to run suites from the CLI.
Visual snapshot
Test classes, test methods, fixtures, and assertions form the core workflow you will practice.
Example
BankAccount tests: verify deposit, withdraw, and error handling with assertEqual and assertRaises.
Try this
Write tests for a palindrome checker that ignore punctuation and case, then run python -m unittest.
Note: this module uses a code-first, live-coding presentation style. Expect code panels and CLI examples in lesson screens.

screens.title: Learning Objectives

You'll be comfortable using setUp and tearDown to create clean test fixtures and using setUpClass and tearDownClass when a shared, expensive resource is required. You will also be able to select and apply assertion methods to express expected outcomes, and run tests or suites from the command line using python -m unittest. Each objective focuses on a practical skill: writing readable tests that run in isolation, verifying exceptions and edge cases with assertRaises, and organizing tests so they are discoverable and maintainable. These objectives matter because well-structured tests speed debugging, document intended behaviour, and make refactoring safer. As you practice, pay attention to small errors like forgetting to inherit from unittest. TestCase, which prevents discovery and removes access to assertion helpers.

screens.title: Objective Details
screens.narratorSegment: Let's make success concrete. Success looks like a test suite of small, focused test methods that each assert a single behaviour, executed reliably by python -m unittest. It looks like setUp creating a fresh BankAccount instance before each test and tearDown removing any temporary files, so tests don't leave artifacts. It also looks like a TestStringUtilities class with tests for mixed case palindromes, punctuation, empty strings, and non-string inputs that raise TypeError. When you reach mastery you'll choose the right assertion for the situation: assertEqual when comparing values, assertTrue for boolean conditions, assertRaises for exceptions, and assertIn for containment checks. Finally, you'll recognize anti-patterns: forgetting to inherit from TestCase, relying on shared mutable state across tests, and writing overly broad setUp routines that hide dependencies. Practically, measure success by running python -m unittest and seeing tests pass deterministically across repeated runs; failures should point to a specific behaviour rather than a test ordering flake.

screens.title: TestCase and test_ methods
screens.narratorSegment: unittest is organized around the TestCase class. A TestCase is a container for related test methods and helper code. To write tests you define a class that inherits from unittest. TestCase, and within it write methods whose names begin with test_. These test_ methods are discovered automatically by unittest's discovery mechanism when you run python -m unittest. Each test method is executed as a separate test case with its own instance of the TestCase class, so instance variables set in one test do not carry to another unless you intentionally use class-level state. This isolation is fundamental: it prevents one failing test from corrupting another due to shared state. A concrete example is creating a BankAccount in a test method, performing deposit, and asserting the new balance with assertEqual. A common misconception is that writing free functions named test_* is sufficient; in unittest they are discovered only if they appear in a class inheriting from TestCase or at module level matching discovery patterns. Finally, always remember to inherit from unittest. TestCase; forgetting that prevents discovery and removes access to helpful assertion methods. How can you design your tests so each one checks a single behaviour and fails clearly when the contract is broken?

keyIdea.title: TestCase pattern
keyIdea.text: Define classes inheriting unittest.TestCase and name methods test_* so each test runs in isolation and is discoverable.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.2 › TestCase and test_ methods
Definition

A TestCase groups related tests. Methods named test_* are executed as separate tests with per-test isolation.

import unittest

class TestBankAccount(unittest.TestCase):
  def test_deposit(self):
    account = BankAccount(100)
    account.deposit(50)
    self.assertEqual(account.balance, 150)
Concrete example
The test_deposit method creates a fresh BankAccount and asserts the expected balance after deposit.
Common mistake
Forgetting to inherit from unittest.TestCase prevents discovery and removes assertion helpers like assertEqual.
Why this matters
  • Each test runs independently, reducing flaky tests caused by shared state.
  • Discovery means you can run many tests with a single command.
  • Assertions provide readable failure messages that help debugging.
Key Takeaway

Write small, focused test_ methods in TestCase classes to get isolated, discoverable tests.

screens.title: Test discovery and running tests
screens.narratorSegment: Running tests with unittest uses a simple discovery rule: files named test_* dot P Y file or *_test dot P Y file are discoverable, and within those modules TestCase classes with test_ methods are executed. The basic command is python -m unittest test_account dot P Y file to run a specific test file, or python -m unittest to run discovery across the current project using default patterns. A good process is: place tests in a tests directory or alongside modules, name files so discovery finds them, and keep tests focused so the output matches a single failing behaviour. For a test run, unittest creates a fresh TestCase instance per test method, calls setUp, runs the test method, then calls tearDown. This lifecycle ensures fixtures are set up and cleaned per test. A misconception is assuming test order is guaranteed; tests may run in file order but should be written to be independent. If you need a reproducible order for a specific diagnostic, rely on explicit test suite construction rather than test ordering. Finally, grouping tests into suites helps run related tests together and avoids long global discovery when you want short focused runs.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.2 › Test discovery and running tests
Quick CLI recipes
Use the following commands to control runs and discovery.
# Run a single file
python -m unittest test_account.py

# Run discovery across project
python -m unittest

# Use discover explicitly
python -m unittest discover -s tests -p "test_*.py"
Naming tests so discovery finds them makes automation and CI integration straightforward. If you need grouped execution, build a TestSuite and run it programmatically.
Lifecycle visual
1. Create TestCase instance
2. Call setUp()
3. Run the test_* method
4. Call tearDown()
Key Takeaway

Name tests for discovery, rely on per-test lifecycle for isolation, and use explicit suites when you need grouped runs.

screens.title: Assertion methods in unittest
screens.narratorSegment: Assertion methods are the language you use inside test methods to express contracts about code behaviour. unittest. TestCase provides many helpers: assertEqual for equality checks, assertTrue and assertFalse for boolean conditions, assertIn for containment, assertIsNone to check None, and assertRaises to verify exceptions. Choosing the right assertion improves failure messages and makes tests easier to debug. For example, use assertEqual(account. balance, 150) rather than assertTrue(account. balance == 150) because assertEqual reports both expected and actual values clearly. A common misconception is overusing assertTrue or assertFalse for everything; prefer specific assertions when available since they yield better diagnostics. Another point is that assertRaises can be used both as a context manager and as a function-style call; the context manager is often clearer when you want to demonstrate which statement should raise. Finally, assertions document intent: if a test uses assertIn it communicates containment; if it uses assertRaises it documents that an error is the correct behaviour here. This clarity helps future readers and maintainers understand why the behaviour matters. Assertion methods in unittest means use specific assertions like assertequal, assertin, and assertraises for clearer tests and more informative failures.. In practical terms, express expectations clearly with the right assertions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.2 › Assertion methods
Common assertions
  • assertEqual(a, b) — compares values and reports both sides on failure.
  • assertTrue(expr) — checks a boolean condition.
  • assertRaises(exc) — verifies an exception is raised.
  • assertIn(member, container) — checks containment.
Diagnostic example
assertEqual produces clearer messages than assertTrue when comparing values, helping you fix the bug faster.
Usage pattern
with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
  account.deposit(0)

self.assertIn('error', log_contents)
self.assertIsNone(result)
Key Takeaway

Prefer specific assertions to improve clarity and failure diagnostics; use assertRaises for exception behaviour.

screens.title: Testing exceptions with assertRaises
screens.narratorSegment: Testing that code raises the expected exception is a common need. unittest offers assertRaises which can be used as a context manager to clearly indicate the exact statement expected to raise. For example, when testing the BankAccount. deposit method, you expect a ValueError if the amount is zero or negative. Using with self. assertRaises(ValueError): account. deposit(0) makes the intent explicit. The context manager form is preferable because it scopes the code under test and avoids accidentally catching exceptions from setup code. You can also use the function-style call assertRaises(ExceptionType, callable, *args) when calling a function directly, but this form can be less expressive in multi-statement scenarios. A common misconception is to wrap multiple unrelated statements in a single assertRaises context; that hides which statement actually raised the exception. Instead, keep the context to the minimal statement. Concrete example: test_deposit_zero_or_negative_amount_raises_error uses two assertRaises blocks to test amount 0 and -10 separately, ensuring each case is verified. Closing takeaway: assertRaises documents expected failure modes; use the context manager narrowly so failures point to the exact operation. Testing exceptions with assertRaises means use assertraises as a context manager around the single statement expected to raise, so failures are precise and intentional.. In practical terms, verify that incorrect inputs raise the right errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use assertRaises as a context manager around the single statement expected to raise, so failures are precise and intentional.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.2 › Testing exceptions with assertRaises
Example test
def test_deposit_zero_or_negative_amount_raises_error(self):
    account = BankAccount(100)
    with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
        account.deposit(0)
    with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
        account.deposit(-10)
Each with block isolates the statement expected to raise, producing clearer failure locations.
Misconception check
Avoid wrapping multiple operations in one assertRaises block. If multiple statements are in the block, you won't know which line caused the exception when the test fails.
Key Takeaway

Use assertRaises as a narrow context manager and test each error condition independently for precise diagnostics.

screens.title: setUp and tearDown for fixtures
screens.narratorSegment: Fixtures are the pieces of state or resources your tests need to run. In unittest you use setUp to create those resources before each test method, and tearDown to clean them up afterward. This pattern enforces isolation and prevents side effects from leaking between tests. A typical use is creating a BankAccount instance and a temporary file in setUp, and deleting that file in tearDown. The chapter example creates a temp_test_log. txt file in setUp, writes initial content, and removes it in tearDown. One misconception is relying on setUpClass for everything; while setUpClass is useful for expensive shared resources like starting a database, it does not provide per-test isolation. Another anti-pattern is a bulky setUp that sets many unrelated resources; this suggests the unit under test is too large and should be refactored or that specific tests should construct only the resources they need. When writing setUp and tearDown, keep them small and predictable. Finally, using setUp ensures that even when a test fails, tearDown still runs, allowing cleanup and preventing leftover artifacts from interfering with subsequent tests. setUp and tearDown for fixtures means use setup and teardown to create and remove per-test resources so tests remain independent and repeatable.. In practical terms, prepare and clean resources before and after each test. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Per-test fixtures
keyIdea.text: Use setUp and tearDown to create and remove per-test resources so tests remain independent and repeatable.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.2 › setUp and tearDown for fixtures
Fixture example
class TestBankAccountAdvanced(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.account = BankAccount(100)
        self.temp_file_name = "temp_test_log.txt"
        with open(self.temp_file_name, 'w') as f:
            f.write("Test started.
")

    def tearDown(self):
        del self.account
        if os.path.exists(self.temp_file_name):
            os.remove(self.temp_file_name)
Why small fixtures help
  • Small setUp makes tests easier to read and reason about.
  • tearDown ensures cleanup even when tests fail, avoiding leftover artifacts.
  • Bulky setUp is a sign the unit may need refactoring or injection of dependencies.
Key Takeaway

Implement focused setUp and tearDown so each test has a clean environment and predictable cleanup.

screens.title: setUpClass and tearDownClass
screens.narratorSegment: When tests need an expensive shared resource, unittest offers setUpClass and tearDownClass class methods that run once before and after all tests in the TestCase class. Use these for resources that are costly to initialize, such as an in-memory database or a persistent connection used by all tests in the class. Mark them with @classmethod and operate on cls, not self. The chapter notes that these methods are useful for expensive, shared resource setup and cleanup. One important clarification: because setUpClass runs once for the class, it does not provide per-test isolation; any mutable state created there should be used carefully or reset in setUp to avoid test interactions. A pitfall is relying solely on setUpClass for everything and forgetting that each test should still be isolated; use setUpClass to create shared read-only fixtures or resources you can reset per test. In practice combine setUpClass for expensive, immutable resources and setUp for per-test state. This hybrid approach balances performance with isolation. setUpClass and tearDownClass means use setupclass and teardownclass for expensive shared resources, but preserve per-test isolation with setup when needed.. In practical terms, managing expensive, shared resources safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Class-level fixtures
keyIdea.text: Use setUpClass and tearDownClass for expensive shared resources, but preserve per-test isolation with setUp when needed.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.2 › setUpClass and tearDownClass
Class-level example
class TestBankAccountAdvanced(unittest.TestCase):
    @classmethod
    def setUpClass(cls):
        cls.shared_resource = 'Database connection object'

    @classmethod
    def tearDownClass(cls):
        del cls.shared_resource
Practical guidance
  • Use for expensive initialization run only once per class.
  • Do not rely on setUpClass for per-test mutable state.
  • Combine with setUp to ensure each test has clean state.
Common pitfall

Putting mutable objects in setUpClass without resetting them per test causes cross-test interference.

screens.title: BankAccount tests in practice

Module 10 › Chapter 10.2 › BankAccount tests
Production: account.py
class BankAccount:
    def __init__(self, initial_balance=0):
        if not isinstance(initial_balance, (int, float)) or initial_balance < 0:
            raise ValueError("Initial balance must be a non-negative number.")
        self.balance = initial_balance

    def deposit(self, amount):
        if not isinstance(amount, (int, float)) or amount <= 0:
            raise ValueError("Deposit amount must be a positive number.")
        self.balance += amount
        return self.balance

    def withdraw(self, amount):
        if not isinstance(amount, (int, float)) or amount <= 0:
            raise ValueError("Withdrawal amount must be a positive number.")
        if amount > self.balance:
            raise ValueError("Insufficient funds.")
        self.balance -= amount
        return self.balance
Tests: test_account.py
import unittest
from account import BankAccount

class TestBankAccount(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_initial_balance(self):
        account = BankAccount(100)
        self.assertEqual(account.balance, 100)

    def test_deposit(self):
        account = BankAccount(100)
        account.deposit(50)
        self.assertEqual(account.balance, 150)

    def test_deposit_zero_or_negative_amount_raises_error(self):
        account = BankAccount(100)
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            account.deposit(0)
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            account.deposit(-10)
Run: python -m unittest test_account.py or python -m unittest for discovery.

screens.title: Common mistakes and anti-patterns
screens.narratorSegment: There are recurring mistakes learners make when adopting unittest. First, forgetting to inherit from unittest. TestCase blocks discovery and removes assertion helpers; always inherit from TestCase. Second, sharing mutable state across tests or having setUp create many unrelated resources leads to test coupling and flakiness; keep fixtures minimal and per-test when possible. Third, wrapping multiple statements in assertRaises or overly broad try/except in tests hides which operation failed; use narrow contexts. Fourth, relying on implicit test order makes tests fragile; write tests that are independent of order or use explicit TestSuite ordering if required. Finally, neglecting cleanup creates artifacts like temporary files or open connections that can influence other tests; always clean up in tearDown or use context managers. When you see long, complex setUp methods, consider refactoring the production code to reduce dependencies or using mocking for external resources. The best practice is small tests, clear assertions, minimal fixtures, and explicit cleanup so failures point directly to the broken behaviour. Module 10 › Chapter 10.2 › StringUtilities palindrome tests
Starter: string_utils.py
import re

class StringUtilities:
    @staticmethod
    def is_palindrome(text):
        if not isinstance(text, str):
            raise TypeError("Input must be a string.")
        cleaned_text = re.sub(r'[^a-z0-9]', '', text.lower())
        return cleaned_text == cleaned_text[::-1]
Tests: test_string_utils.py (starter)
import unittest
from string_utils import StringUtilities

class TestStringUtilities(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_basic_palindrome(self):
        self.assertTrue(StringUtilities.is_palindrome("madam"))

    def test_non_palindrome(self):
        self.assertFalse(StringUtilities.is_palindrome("hello"))

    # Add tests for mixed case, punctuation, empty string, single char, and invalid input.

if __name__ == '__main__':

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you'll build fluency with Python's built-in unittest framework and learn why xUnit-style tests matter for robust, maintainable code. We will explore the TestCase pattern, the convention of test_ methods used by discovery, and a broad set of assertion helpers that let you express expectations clearly. You'll also learn how to manage test fixtures with setUp and tearDown so each test runs in isolation, and when to use class-level setup for expensive shared resources. Along the way we practice with concrete examples: a BankAccount class for numeric operations and a StringUtilities palindrome checker for string edge cases. By mastering unittest you gain a standard-library skill that helps debug regressions, document intended behaviour, and support continuous integration. This lesson prepares you to write focused tests, avoid common mistakes like forgetting to inherit from TestCase, and organize tests so they run smoothly from the command line. As you move forward, ask yourself: does each test verify one behavior and clean up after itself?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to write TestCase classes using unittest and understand why the test_ naming convention enables automatic discovery. You'll be comfortable using setUp and tearDown to create clean test fixtures and using setUpClass and tearDownClass when a shared, expensive resource is required. You will also be able to select and apply assertion methods to express expected outcomes, and run tests or suites from the command line using python -m unittest. Each objective focuses on a practical skill: writing readable tests that run in isolation, verifying exceptions and edge cases with assertRaises, and organizing tests so they are discoverable and maintainable. These objectives matter because well-structured tests speed debugging, document intended behaviour, and make refactoring safer. As you practice, pay attention to small errors like forgetting to inherit from unittest. TestCase, which prevents discovery and removes access to assertion helpers.

Let's make success concrete. Success looks like a test suite of small, focused test methods that each assert a single behaviour, executed reliably by python -m unittest. It looks like setUp creating a fresh BankAccount instance before each test and tearDown removing any temporary files, so tests don't leave artifacts. It also looks like a TestStringUtilities class with tests for mixed case palindromes, punctuation, empty strings, and non-string inputs that raise TypeError. When you reach mastery you'll choose the right assertion for the situation: assertEqual when comparing values, assertTrue for boolean conditions, assertRaises for exceptions, and assertIn for containment checks. Finally, you'll recognize anti-patterns: forgetting to inherit from TestCase, relying on shared mutable state across tests, and writing overly broad setUp routines that hide dependencies. Practically, measure success by running python -m unittest and seeing tests pass deterministically across repeated runs; failures should point to a specific behaviour rather than a test ordering flake.

unittest is organized around the TestCase class. A TestCase is a container for related test methods and helper code. To write tests you define a class that inherits from unittest. TestCase, and within it write methods whose names begin with test_. These test_ methods are discovered automatically by unittest's discovery mechanism when you run python -m unittest. Each test method is executed as a separate test case with its own instance of the TestCase class, so instance variables set in one test do not carry to another unless you intentionally use class-level state. This isolation is fundamental: it prevents one failing test from corrupting another due to shared state. A concrete example is creating a BankAccount in a test method, performing deposit, and asserting the new balance with assertEqual. A common misconception is that writing free functions named test_* is sufficient; in unittest they are discovered only if they appear in a class inheriting from TestCase or at module level matching discovery patterns. Finally, always remember to inherit from unittest. TestCase; forgetting that prevents discovery and removes access to helpful assertion methods. How can you design your tests so each one checks a single behaviour and fails clearly when the contract is broken?

Running tests with unittest uses a simple discovery rule: files named test_* dot P Y file or *_test dot P Y file are discoverable, and within those modules TestCase classes with test_ methods are executed. The basic command is python -m unittest test_account dot P Y file to run a specific test file, or python -m unittest to run discovery across the current project using default patterns. A good process is: place tests in a tests directory or alongside modules, name files so discovery finds them, and keep tests focused so the output matches a single failing behaviour. For a test run, unittest creates a fresh TestCase instance per test method, calls setUp, runs the test method, then calls tearDown. This lifecycle ensures fixtures are set up and cleaned per test. A misconception is assuming test order is guaranteed; tests may run in file order but should be written to be independent. If you need a reproducible order for a specific diagnostic, rely on explicit test suite construction rather than test ordering. Finally, grouping tests into suites helps run related tests together and avoids long global discovery when you want short focused runs.

Assertion methods are the language you use inside test methods to express contracts about code behaviour. unittest. TestCase provides many helpers: assertEqual for equality checks, assertTrue and assertFalse for boolean conditions, assertIn for containment, assertIsNone to check None, and assertRaises to verify exceptions. Choosing the right assertion improves failure messages and makes tests easier to debug. For example, use assertEqual(account. balance, 150) rather than assertTrue(account. balance == 150) because assertEqual reports both expected and actual values clearly. A common misconception is overusing assertTrue or assertFalse for everything; prefer specific assertions when available since they yield better diagnostics. Another point is that assertRaises can be used both as a context manager and as a function-style call; the context manager is often clearer when you want to demonstrate which statement should raise. Finally, assertions document intent: if a test uses assertIn it communicates containment; if it uses assertRaises it documents that an error is the correct behaviour here. This clarity helps future readers and maintainers understand why the behaviour matters. Assertion methods in unittest means use specific assertions like assertequal, assertin, and assertraises for clearer tests and more informative failures.. In practical terms, express expectations clearly with the right assertions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Testing that code raises the expected exception is a common need. unittest offers assertRaises which can be used as a context manager to clearly indicate the exact statement expected to raise. For example, when testing the BankAccount. deposit method, you expect a ValueError if the amount is zero or negative. Using with self. assertRaises(ValueError): account. deposit(0) makes the intent explicit. The context manager form is preferable because it scopes the code under test and avoids accidentally catching exceptions from setup code. You can also use the function-style call assertRaises(ExceptionType, callable, *args) when calling a function directly, but this form can be less expressive in multi-statement scenarios. A common misconception is to wrap multiple unrelated statements in a single assertRaises context; that hides which statement actually raised the exception. Instead, keep the context to the minimal statement. Concrete example: test_deposit_zero_or_negative_amount_raises_error uses two assertRaises blocks to test amount 0 and -10 separately, ensuring each case is verified. Closing takeaway: assertRaises documents expected failure modes; use the context manager narrowly so failures point to the exact operation. Testing exceptions with assertRaises means use assertraises as a context manager around the single statement expected to raise, so failures are precise and intentional.. In practical terms, verify that incorrect inputs raise the right errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Fixtures are the pieces of state or resources your tests need to run. In unittest you use setUp to create those resources before each test method, and tearDown to clean them up afterward. This pattern enforces isolation and prevents side effects from leaking between tests. A typical use is creating a BankAccount instance and a temporary file in setUp, and deleting that file in tearDown. The chapter example creates a temp_test_log. txt file in setUp, writes initial content, and removes it in tearDown. One misconception is relying on setUpClass for everything; while setUpClass is useful for expensive shared resources like starting a database, it does not provide per-test isolation. Another anti-pattern is a bulky setUp that sets many unrelated resources; this suggests the unit under test is too large and should be refactored or that specific tests should construct only the resources they need. When writing setUp and tearDown, keep them small and predictable. Finally, using setUp ensures that even when a test fails, tearDown still runs, allowing cleanup and preventing leftover artifacts from interfering with subsequent tests. setUp and tearDown for fixtures means use setup and teardown to create and remove per-test resources so tests remain independent and repeatable.. In practical terms, prepare and clean resources before and after each test. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When tests need an expensive shared resource, unittest offers setUpClass and tearDownClass class methods that run once before and after all tests in the TestCase class.
